Publisher XML full text converted with jats_text (section and paragraph locators)

entry.evidence: It is still not well-understood how the pixel-to-pixel intensity variations relate to the variation in ridging.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: Pose the open question of how SAR pixel intensity variation relates to ice ridging, motivated by the need for quantitative ridging parameters beyond the qualitative DIR numeral.
steps.quote: It is still not well-understood how the pixel-to-pixel intensity variations relate to the variation in ridging.

steps.action: Assemble a 2011 TerraSAR-X ScanSAR image (20 m), a 2016 stripmap image (1.25 m) and 2800 km of helicopter lidar surface profiles, identifying ridge sails by the Rayleigh criterion above a 0.4 m cutoff.
steps.quote: Two modes of TerraSAR-X (TSX) satellite data were used.

steps.action: Record the ambient conditions found at acquisition (cold, dry snow, sub-zero temperatures) and assume dry snow did not affect backscattering.
steps.quote: It can be assumed that during the ScanSAR acquisition prior to the campaign, the snow was still dry

steps.action: Define the bright-pixel approach: select a bright-pixel percentage (BPP) by an intensity threshold and count bright-pixel numbers (BPNs) in blocks of side length L.
steps.quote: Towards this end, a certain bright-pixel percentage (BPP) is selected with an intensity threshold.

steps.action: Design the validation around linear lidar profiles, counting ridge sail numbers (RSNs) in segments of length L, because areal scanning lidar data are too limited.
steps.quote: The validation data, therefore, consist of linear surface profiles from which ridge sails are identified.

steps.action: Derive ridge rubble coverage from observed ridge density (about 2 % per unit density), using an adopted width/height ratio R = 13 and the authors' earlier cutoff-extrapolation model (Lensu 2003).
steps.quote: To include the contribution of these, the value R = 13 is adopted.

steps.action: Formulate the threshold process, in which pixels or sails are added as the threshold falls, and randomly permute values above the target threshold to reduce it to a random deposition process.
steps.quote: The random permutation has the merit of removing the spatial correlations of intensities or sail heights

steps.action: Adopt the linear generative hypothesis (increase probability proportional to n + aL) from earlier work, which yields hypergeometric, negative binomial and gamma distributions as a scale system.
steps.quote: The simplest assumption satisfying the condition is

steps.action: Specify a two-stage test: check that increase rates depend linearly on RSN or BPN, then fit the distributions by mean and variance and check goodness of fit across scales.
steps.quote: The statistical model is validated in two stages.

steps.action: Build a SAR texture simulation: a random scale cascade with weights aN0 + N1 adds white pixels to a low-BPP seed image.
steps.quote: A binary image with value 1 (white) for an observed low percentage of brightest pixels is used to seed the process.

steps.action: Compute RSN increase rates for randomised and original sail heights (target 0.5 m, L = 50-800 m); randomised rates are near-linear, and the deviation in the original data is attributed to sail height correlations, which are confirmed.
steps.quote: The increase rates were linear with a slight superlinear bend.

steps.action: Fit negative binomial and hypergeometric distributions to the RSN data and find good agreement, except that empty segments are overestimated at 200 and 400 m.
steps.quote: The hypergeometric and negative binomial distributions were fitted to the data with observed mean and variance.

steps.action: Find that parameter a decreases with L as a power law (exponent about 0.5) and interpret this as fractal geometry of the rubble-covered area.
steps.quote: Thus the power law suggests that the area covered by ridge rubble has fractal geometry.

steps.action: Introduce contextual images (convolution with an L x L all-ones kernel) and category images (brightest 30 % split into three classes).
steps.quote: This is accomplished by a convolution with an L × L all-ones kernel.

steps.action: Observe in the 1.25 m stripmap image that ridges appear as chains of detached bright components, with texture similar to ship channels, rather than as continuous linear features.
steps.quote: There are obvious linear ridges, but these consist of chains of detached bright components that do not connect to continuous features.

steps.action: Compare the observed randomness with published backscatter models (Manninen 1992; Carlström and Ulander 1995) and take it as support for bright-pixel density being proportional to rubble coverage.
steps.quote: bright returns from ridge rubble depend on random factors like a favourable orientation of blocks

steps.action: Run the BPN threshold process on a 7000 x 7000 subimage with permuted intensities (L = 32, BPP 5-40 %) and find linear increase rates until blocks saturate.
steps.quote: Linearity is observed unless the saturation of the pixel block is felt after three-quarters of the block capacity is filled.

steps.action: Vary the block side length from 4 to 128 at BPP 20 % and compare randomised with original intensities; the results are similar, with non-linearity in the original data attributed to intensity correlations.
steps.quote: The results are similar to the first test case.

steps.action: Fit negative binomial and hypergeometric models to BPN distributions on a 9216 x 9216 subimage and find good agreement, with power-law exponents of a (-0.45 to -0.37) close to the RSN values.
steps.quote: The agreement of the proposed distribution system with the data is again good.

steps.action: Simulate a BPP 13 % image from the BPP 3 % seed of a 1024 x 1024 subimage using the cascade algorithm.
steps.quote: The simulation added 10 % so that the resulting BPP is 13 %.

steps.action: Because the Poisson component produced dispersion and spurious clusters, add a support restriction (threshold Co, area limits N1-N2) to the simulation rather than change the generative hypothesis.
steps.quote: To reduce this, an additional condition requires that in a process step, a white pixel cannot be added within a rectangle

steps.action: Compare simulated and real 13 % images: they are not identical pixel by pixel, but their density variations, contextual images and category images at L = 21 match almost exactly.
steps.quote: The results provide additional corroboration for the soundness of the generative hypothesis.

steps.action: Estimate SAR rubble coverage from the 20 m ScanSAR image (BPP 20 %, 15 x 15 contextual image, averaged to 1 km2) and lidar rubble coverage as ridge density times 2 % in matching grid cells.
steps.quote: As the target is rubble coverage, the BPN values are changed to percentage points.

steps.action: Because ice drifted between the SAR acquisition and the flights, design the comparison as regional (distribution against distribution) instead of cell-by-cell pairing.
steps.quote: it is not possible to establish a pairing between the two RRC estimates in SAR analysis pixels and lidar grid cells

steps.action: Compare SAR and lidar rubble-coverage distributions in a Q-Q plot and find a near-linear relation with slope 1.34, consistent with gamma distributions sharing a shape parameter.
steps.quote: The quantile pairs are largely located along a line with a ratio of 1.34 between the quantiles

steps.action: Scale SAR coverage by 1.34, obtaining means of 26.2 % versus 25.9 % (about 13 ridges per km), and fit gamma distributions by maximum likelihood (shape 1.7 vs 1.4; scale 15.5 vs 18.2).
steps.quote: Thus, although the parameters of the fits are close to each other, they are not equal.

steps.action: Attribute the tail mismatch (Q-Q no longer linear above 50 % SAR and 75 % lidar coverage, lidar rubble-field hump) to oversampling of the coastal rubble field by the flights.
steps.quote: With a spatially more uniform coverage of the lidar flights over the SAR image, the agreement would probably have been better for the tail part.

steps.action: Vary the SAR area (scaling 1.3-1.6) and BPP (10, 15 and 20 % give scaling 2.22, 1.61 and 1.34); the Q-Q plot stays linear and the scaled means stay close to the lidar mean.
steps.quote: In all three cases, the Q–Q plot is linear for its main part

steps.action: Show that category contextual images are nearly unchanged across BPP 2-95 %, across alternative contextual methods (sliding-block intensity average) and after multiplying the image eight times by a random matrix, and quantify this with pixel-to-pixel mapping.
steps.quote: The same result is found for several alternative methods to generate a contextual image

steps.action: Conclude that the distribution model applies to both BPN and RSN and that the method gives ridge density up to a scaling factor, to be supplied by independent data such as ICESat-2.
steps.quote: demonstrated that the method can be used to derive ridge density up to the scaling factor

steps.action: Propose that the hypergeometric model and the lognormal sail-spacing model (Kolmogorov breakup) share a physical origin in ridge formation events.
steps.quote: This indicates that the applicability of lognormal and that of hypergeometric models have the same physical origin.

tree.answer: Yes; many blocks and segments across scales, thresholds and two data types
Yes across BPP, L, area, method and randomisation; tail mismatch remains
Model kept; ridge density retrievable up to a scaling factor

end.claim: A threshold-process scale system of negative binomial/hypergeometric distributions describes bright-pixel numbers and ridge sail numbers over a wide range of BPP and L, and SAR- and lidar-derived rubble coverage follow the same distribution apart from a scaling factor.

decisive_move.sentence: Fitting the scale-system distributions to the high-resolution BPN data, and finding them consistent with the RSN fits, is what links bright-pixel density to ridge density.

gates.evidence: The images (2011, 2016) and lidar profiles came from earlier acquisitions and a campaign not directed by the threshold-process hypothesis (inference). Linearity of increase rates, distribution fits, the simulation and the Q-Q linearity could have failed, but goodness of fit is judged visually and the scaling factor (1.34) is fitted to the same data. The two-stage validation is stated in Methods (§2.5 ¶5) with no evidence it was fixed before the data were seen, and the simulation parameters were 'determined by simple experimentation' (§3.4 ¶2).

imports.item: Hypergeometric, negative binomial and gamma distributions as a scale system
Quantile-quantile plot as a nonparametric distribution comparison
Random deposition (Poisson) process obtained by random permutation
Fractal geometry of the rubble-covered area
Kolmogorov (1941) breakup process giving lognormal sizes
Rayleigh criterion for separating successive maxima
Convolution with an all-ones kernel to produce contextual images

novelty_claims.quote: The present paper provides a model that connects SAR image statistics with ridging statistics.
This provided a statistical connection between the bright-pixel density and the ridge density.

limits: No review file or discussion was supplied, although the paper was open-review (two anonymous referees), so no review sequence is coded and tree question 9 is unanswered. No quantitative goodness-of-fit statistics are reported; agreement is judged visually from figures. The high- and medium-resolution images do not overlap in space or time, and the lidar-SAR comparison is regional because ice drifted. The tail of the coverage distribution does not match, which the authors attribute to sampling, untested. Sub-claims: ridge density derivable up to a scaling factor (1.34 at BPP 20 %, 1.3-1.6 depending on area, 2.22 at BPP 10 %) is estimate_with_resolution; insensitivity of contextual category images to BPP, method and randomisation is capability_characterized; fractal rubble geometry and the shared lognormal/hypergeometric origin are suggestions with status none; C- and L-band applicability and wet-snow conditions are untested hypotheses (§4 ¶5). The simulation parameters were tuned by experimentation. The RRC conversion rests on rough adopted factors (R = 13, 2 %). That the data were not collected for this hypothesis is inference.

disagreements.target: Dumitru and Datcu (2013), quasi-photorealistic TerraSAR-X terrestrial images
disagreements.support: In the 1.25 m sea-ice stripmap image, ridges appear as chains of detached bright components rather than delineated features.
disagreements.quote: The hope of a similar quasi-photorealistic appearance as is found in comparable TerraSAR-X terrestrial images by does [...] .

disagreements.target: SAR ice type classification approaches relying on tail intensity variations
disagreements.support: Contextual images are nearly unchanged across BPP values, which suggests weak correlation between sail height and SAR intensity.
disagreements.quote: The tail intensity variations, which are often relied on in SAR ice type classification approaches, were left to play a secondary role.

disagreements.target: Degree of ice ridging (DIR) numeral in Finnish-Swedish ice charts
disagreements.support: The paper offers bright-pixel density as a quantitative proxy for rubble coverage and ridge density instead of a qualitative numeral.
disagreements.quote: Due to the qualitative nature of DIR, a need for SAR methods to retrieve quantitative ridging parameters persists.
